skip_reason: Existing-move logistics only — not a sales call. Inbound date-change request on an already-booked job, the same pattern skipped for this rep on 8/31. The customer opens by asking for the rep he had been working with ('My name is Emanuel and I was previously working with Bree. Is she available by chance?') and states his position immediately: 'I have a scheduled move date right now for the... the twenty second but I was wondering if it was possible to move up [my] move date to the seventeenth.' The entire call is Jespah checking cross-branch availability, comparing day-of-week rates and revised totals across five candidate dates, and moving the existing booking from the twenty-second to Sunday the twentieth. There is no quote being built and no sale being made — the estimate, the arrival time (8:30) and the crew size all pre-exist and carry over unchanged ('start time exactly the same. Everything stays the same except we're moving in up by to, to the Sunday instead'). No probe, no home-size or access questions, no inclusions or differentiator pitch, no clock explanation, no Save Your Ass, no booking attempt and no deposit conversation, because none of those are in scope on a date change. Scoring the nine-section scorecard here would produce a meaningless number on a call the rep handled well.
top_strength: Jespah picked up another rep's customer cold and handled it so cleanly that the customer never asked for Bree again. Her opening move was the right one — she tried to get him the person he asked for ('I'm texting her right now. Give me a second here [Emanuel]') and then, rather than leaving him in dead air, opened a lane for herself without making it a takeover: 'I sent her a message. I'll give her a couple of seconds to respond to see if she's actually at her desk or not I guess in the meantime, you can ask me a question. Maybe I can just answer directly for you.' That is warm-transfer etiquette done properly, and it turned a hold into a completed change. She then did something genuinely customer-first that most reps would skip: she went looking for a way to save him money that nobody asked her to look for. The seventeenth was available only through North Austin, and instead of just selling him that, she named the cost and then went hunting for a workaround: 'the only thing is that it's at the north Austin branch... so that would, that would just introduce a travel fee that we can avoid that we keep it at the south Austin branch but sometimes I can actually move stuff around between branches, so I'm taking a look to see if actually there's a spot I can open up on the seventeenth.' When it did not work, she said so plainly and priced the alternative honestly rather than burying it — 'it looks like unfortunately, everything's booked out in a way where I can't move things between branches so we could do it through north Austin it would, it would increase the price by $150 so if that days, if that's worth that to you we can do it if not, we can keep you where you're at.' Her rate transparency across the week is the best thing on the call: she walked him through the twenty-second at $208 an hour, Sunday the twentieth at $210, the nineteenth as the most expensive day at $222, then checked the eighteenth when he asked and gave it at the same $222 as Saturday — and crucially she converted rates into totals so he could actually decide: '$1,352 for the twenty second. If we move it to Friday it would be $1,443 for the total estimate,' and then on the Sunday option, 'It goes from $1,352 to 1365 so a $7 difference there.' A customer choosing between five dates got the dollar consequence of each one, which is why he could decide in seconds ('Yeah, very nominal. Let's, let's do that'). She was also completely unhurried while he checked three work calendars — 'Sure, sure. Yeah, no rush at all' — and closed the loop the right way, confirming the arrival time carried over, committing to the updated confirmation ('I'll send you an updated confirmation email with the changes there which again is gonna be just the date'), and leaving the door open: 'if you need us for any reason before then though just give us a call. We'll be here.'
coaching_note: Not scored — date change on a booked job, outside the sales average. Jespah handled it very well; these are refinements. First, the one real miss, and it is a small one with an outsized effect: the customer had to ask for her name at the end of the call. 'I'm so sorry. I don't think I fully caught your name at the beginning. What was your name?' She had opened with it, but it did not land, and her answer — 'my name is Jesper and it will be at the bottom of the email that I'm about to send you' — deflected to the email instead of owning the moment. This is a customer who opened the call asking for a specific rep by name, which tells you he values the relationship, and he just spent eight minutes with someone new who solved his problem. That was the moment to claim the account: 'It's Jespah — J-E-S-P-A-H, and I'll be at the bottom of that email. Ask for me directly next time, I've got your file now.' She earned that and did not take it. Second, she never asked him to verify the confirmation. The only thing changing is the date, which makes it low-risk, but a date is also the one field on this record that has now moved twice and the entire call was about getting it right. 'It'll land in a few minutes — just glance at the date up top and reply if it's not showing Sunday the twentieth' costs three seconds. Third, a note on framing rather than a fault: he asked whether weekends carry increased fees and she answered with rates ('it is an increase fee for the weekends right now on the twenty second it's $208 an hour. On Sunday, it's not a dramatic increase, it's $210'). Accurate and honest, and her 'that's fairly comfortable' read was fair. But the value-days story never got told — nobody said Tuesday through Thursday is the cheapest way to move, which is what the customer had actually half-remembered from his prior rep ('I think she was saying like Tuesdays and Thursday so like, typically slower days'). He had the idea and nobody confirmed it for him. On a date-change call that is a genuinely useful thing to say, because it is the only lever he controls. For Amanda: one small data point on cross-branch capacity. Jespah tried to shuffle a job between South and North Austin to avoid a $150 travel fee and could not, because 'everything's booked out in a way where I can't move things between branches' in mid-September. That is the second week running that a branch has had no mid-week capacity within its own service area. Worth a look alongside the pacing report if reps are routinely quoting a $150 premium or losing dates outright to availability rather than to price.
phone_presence_notes: Warm, patient and visibly on the customer's side — she hunted for a cross-branch workaround to save him a fee nobody asked her to save, gave him genuine room while he checked three work calendars ('Sure, sure. Yeah, no rush at all'), and closed with real energy ('Awesome! Yeah. It's my pleasure. We're looking forward to it') — short of a 5 because her name never landed until he had to ask for it, and she handed that moment off to the email signature instead of taking it.
